## New Cross-Domain Connection

- **[2026-10-09] Cooking's weekly recipe recommender is the only part of the wiki that decides what Fred actually eats, and it has never read Health. Health's main dementia source sets a food target that the 42 suggestions so far mostly miss.** [[health/source-wood-brain-sharp-2026]] names B vitamins plus omega-3 as "the pair that matters", with targets of 2–4 g EPA+DHA a day and an Omega-3 Index above 8%. [[health/my-protocol]]'s Diet section is still "[to be added]", and [[cooking/cooking-overview]]'s Focus todo still lists "dietary approach" as undefined. Meanwhile [[cooking/recipe-suggestions]] has produced 42 dishes since 06-30. Only two are oily-fish mains: Grilled Mackerel (week of 07-20) and Seared Trout (week of 07-27). Nothing in the eleven weeks since has been oily fish. This week's Moules au Cidre is the first suggestion since July that hits both halves of the pair. Mussels are among the richest food sources of B12, with some EPA+DHA as well (general nutrition knowledge, not from a wiki source). That makes it a better fit for the Health page than anything the recommender has aimed for on purpose. **Why it matters:** the two empty pages could fill each other. Writing one line into my-protocol's Diet section (e.g. "oily fish or shellfish twice a week") would give the recommender a rule to follow, such as one omega-3 or B12 slot per weekly batch. Every Friday's batch would then double as the Health protocol in practice, instead of rotating the same three chefs with no goal.

## New Investigation Ideas
- **[2026-10-08] Lightfin's book track has had an open "self-publish or traditional?" todo since April. Its existing art pipeline is Midjourney, and that choice carries two rules the page never mentions: Amazon KDP's AI-content disclosure and the US rule that purely AI-generated images can't be copyrighted. Today's Creative Penn recommendation is the source built for exactly this question.** [[lightfin/adaptation-overview]] Track 1 (unchanged since 2026-04-25) asks "Self-publish or traditional publisher?" and "Same illustrator for both formats?", with a `[!todo]` to compare KDP, IngramSpark and querying agents. The only illustration work in the wiki is [[lightfin/video-prompts-ep101-poseidons-trident]]: scene prompts in "children's book illustration style" with a Midjourney `--v 6` suffix. That is a picture book's art, already half made. Two outside facts change the decision. First, KDP asks publishers to declare AI-generated text or images when they publish (AI used only for editing or brainstorming need not be declared). Second, the US Copyright Office's *Zarya of the Dawn* decision (2023), upheld in principle by *Thaler v. Perlmutter* (D.C. Cir., 2025), says Midjourney images get no copyright protection; only the human-written text and the arrangement do. For a series whose value is its characters, unprotected character art matters more than for a one-off book. The traditional route has its own constraint, since many children's publishers won't take AI-illustrated submissions. [[podcasts/suggestions]] (week of 2026-10-08) recommends The Creative Penn because Joanna Penn covers "indie publishing plus AI-assisted creative work" and "where to draw the line with AI". Concrete step: listen to one Creative Penn episode on AI disclosure or rights, then add a "Rights & AI" row to Track 1's Key Questions. Options to compare: Midjourney art declared on KDP; a human illustrator for the characters with AI used only for backgrounds; or AI images as a brief for a hired artist. Check the current KDP rule text before relying on it.

## New Cross-Domain Connections
- **[2026-10-08] Strategy A picks its stocks with Greenblatt's Magic Formula and then trades them in a way his own book, already summarised in Books, says will destroy the return: it caps the winners at +25%/+50% and the capital-cap rule cuts the losers at about 54 days. Strategy A's 1-in-10 win rate measures that holding rule, not the formula.** [[books/book-little-book-beats-market]] gives the rules: buy 20–30 names equal-weight, hold about a year, then re-rank and rotate. Its "Why the Formula Keeps Working" section adds that gains are "back-loaded: concentrated in periodic sharp recoveries" and that the formula lags about one year in four. Strategy A's trades ([[finance/paper-trading/trades/2026-09-22-IAG]], -DECK, -MO and -WISE, each citing its Magic Formula rank) do the opposite at both ends. They sell a third at +25% (T1) and another third at +50% (T2), which trims the sharp recoveries that carry the formula's return. At the other end, [[finance/models/model-portfolio-management]] shows Strategy A at 1/10 wins, with PEP, NVO, CMCSA and OTIS cut at −7% to −12% after about 54 days. The same page records the clearest case: NVO, cut at −11.6% on 09-28, passed the Magic Formula screen again on 10-02, rated cheaper and higher quality than when A bought it. Under Greenblatt's rotation rule that is a keep, not a sell. This is narrower than the 09-28 Pzena connection (value books must tolerate losers) and the 10-04 forward-return idea (measure edge apart from exits). The point here is that the strategy's own source document already specifies the holding rules, so no new ~90-day minimum needs inventing. Possible fix: run Strategy A as a Greenblatt cohort (no T1/T2 trims, exempt from the capital cap until 12 months or until it drops out of the top screen ranks) and judge it on cohort return, not win rate. Today's Excess Returns recommendation ([[podcasts/suggestions]], 2026-10-08) is hosted by Validea, which runs guru models including a Greenblatt one. It could give an outside view of how often a properly held Magic Formula book has a 1-in-10 stretch.
